target.title: VID2SPEECH: SPEECH RECONSTRUCTION FROM SILENT VIDEO
target.venue: Not stated on the paper's first page

entries.text: The paper presents an end-to-end CNN pipeline that predicts acoustic features from silent video and synthesizes a speech waveform.
entries.condition: Framewise CNN prediction of speech features, followed by waveform synthesis.

entries.text: The authors claim state-of-the-art GRID word intelligibility and promising OOV-word results.
entries.condition: Author claim in the abstract; reported experiments use GRID.

entries.text: Audio features from the naturally paired signal provide supervision without explicit manual labels.
entries.condition: The predicted feature target is derived from the audio paired with each video sequence.

entries.text: The authors argue that feature regression avoids requiring word- or sub-word segmentation.
entries.condition: Claim about the learning formulation, not a measured comparison in this paper.

entries.text: The authors describe regression as vocabulary-agnostic and argue it can reconstruct words absent from training; they note sub-word classification can also do so.
entries.condition: The paper qualifies its contrast by acknowledging that sub-word classification can also generalize to unseen words.
entries.quote: A regression-based model is also vocabulary-agnostic.

entries.text: The authors state that the representation can reconstruct non-textual speech attributes such as emotion and prosody; this is not evaluated here.
entries.condition: General claimed advantage; no emotion or prosody measure is reported.

entries.text: The authors claim that using the entire face rather than only the mouth improves performance and that temporal context helps disambiguate mouth movements.
entries.condition: Figure 2 compares full-face input with a hard-masked mouth region and varies temporal clip length.

entries.text: The best full-face configuration has lower test error than the best mouth-region configuration.
entries.condition: Both best configurations use K=9 frames; the paper does not identify the exact test split or define the plotted error metric in this comparison.

entries.text: Temporal input length was tested at K=1, 3, 5, 7, and 9; the target always corresponds to the center frame.
entries.condition: The authors say the largest performance gain occurred from K=1 to K=3.

entries.text: The audio target concatenates two successive 9-element LSP vectors into an 18-dimensional feature vector per video frame.
entries.condition: Each underlying LSP vector has 9 elements; two successive vectors are concatenated for one video frame.

entries.text: Audio is downsampled to 8 kHz, framed at 40 ms (320 samples) with 20 ms overlap, analyzed with 8th-order LPC, then decomposed into LSP features.
entries.value: 8 kHz; 40 ms; 320 samples; 20 ms; 8th order; 9 LSP coefficients/frame
entries.condition: The authors chose 8th-order LPC to match the comparator's representation and isolate the visual-feature effect.

entries.text: Audio-feature vectors are standardized element-wise by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.
entries.condition: The text does not specify which partition supplies the means and standard deviations.

entries.text: The source partition for the audio normalization statistics is not stated; it is unclear whether statistics are fit on training data only or include validation/test data.
entries.condition: Applies to the element-wise mean and standard deviation used for the audio target features.

entries.text: The CNN input is a clip of consecutive grayscale frames with the speaker's face cropped and scaled to 128×128 pixels.
entries.condition: The clip contains K frames; its output target is the sound features for the center frame.
entries.quote:
Therefore, the input to our network is a clip
of K consecutive grayscale video frames, out of which the
speaker’s face is cropped and scaled to128× 128 pixels.

entries.text: Video input is divided by maximum pixel intensity and mean-centered.
entries.condition: The text does not identify whether the maximum intensity or mean is estimated per frame, per video, or on a training-only partition.

entries.text: The source and scope of the video normalization maximum and mean are not specified, so train/test normalization leakage cannot be assessed from the text.
entries.condition: Concerns maximum-intensity division and mean subtraction for video inputs.

entries.text: The predictor is a VGG-like CNN with five conv3–conv3–maxpool blocks and filter counts 32–32–64–128–128.
entries.condition: Input is the normalized 128×128×K grayscale face clip; target is the 18-dimensional audio representation.

entries.text: Adam is used with learning rate 0.003.
entries.condition: CNN is trained by backpropagation with mean squared error.

entries.text: Dropout rates are 0.25 after convolutional layers and 0.5 after fully connected layers.
entries.unit: dropout probability after convolutional; fully connected layers
entries.condition: Used as overfitting prevention during CNN training.

entries.text: Training uses batches of 32 samples and stops when validation loss ceases decreasing, at around 80 epochs.
entries.condition: The validation partition and its relation to the train/test split are not described.

entries.text: The paper describes the GRID audiovisual corpus as containing 1,000 sentences from 34 talkers, 18 male and 16 female.
entries.unit: sentences; talkers; male talkers; female talkers
entries.condition: Corpus-wide overview; not the size of the paper's S4 experimental training partition.

entries.text: GRID contains 51 distinct words.
entries.condition: GRID sentences use the six-slot grammar shown in Table 1; the slot count is documented separately.

entries.text: GRID videos are 3 seconds long at 25 FPS, resolution 720×576, and 75 frames per sequence.
entries.condition: Corpus video characteristics stated before experimental preprocessing.

entries.text: The comparison experiments use 1,000 videos from GRID speaker S4, identified as female.
entries.condition: The main random split is within this single speaker; the S2 result is a separate retraining experiment.
entries.quote:
In order to accurately compare our results with [10], we
performed our experiments on the1000 videos of speaker four
(S4, female) as done there.

entries.text: For the full-dataset task, the model is trained/tested with a random 80/20 split of the 1,000 S4 videos.
entries.condition: Video-level random split, same speaker in train and test; audio-only and audio-visual listening configurations are evaluated. Word coverage in both partitions is recorded separately.

entries.text: The random seed and number of repeated runs for the 80/20 S4 split are not stated; no variance across repeated runs is reported.
entries.condition: Applies to the full-dataset S4 experiment and its Table 2 scores.
entries.quote: For this task we trained our model on a random 80/20 train/test split

entries.text: Training stops on validation loss, but the paper does not state how validation data are selected or whether they are separate from the stated train/test split.
entries.condition: The source and size of validation data, and whether they are held out from the 80% training partition, are unspecified.

entries.text: For Figure 2, the exact test set, split, error definition, selection procedure for K, and random seed are not reported.
entries.condition: Figure 2 reports test error by clip length and face/mouth input but does not identify its dataset or evaluation protocol.
entries.quote:
The two
lines in the graph represent ﬁnal network test error as a func-
tion of the length K of the clip used as input to the CNN.

entries.text: MTurk jobs transcribe one of three clip types: audio-only, audio-visual, or OOV audio-visual; listeners are unaware of the clip-type differences.
entries.condition: Each clip is 3 seconds long; word-choice transcription is the human evaluation protocol.
entries.quote: Each job consisted of transcribing one of three types of 3-second clips: audio-only, audio-visual and OOV audio-visual.

entries.text: Listeners receive the GRID vocabulary and classify every reconstructed word among its possible choices; this is a constrained human recognition task, not an unconstrained transcription.
entries.condition: Applies to all three listening-study clip types, including the held-out digit test.
entries.quote:
For each clip, they were given
the GRID vocabulary and tasked with classifying each recon-
structed word into one of its possible options.

entries.text: Across the listening study, more than 400 videos with 38 distinct sequences were transcribed by 23 MTurk workers.
entries.condition: Counts are reported in aggregate across the study, not broken down by clip type or result row.
entries.quote:
All together, over 400 videos containing 38 distinct sequences were tran-
scribed by 23 different MTurk workers, which is comparable
to the 20-listener study done by [10].

entries.text: The target paper says the cited [10] study used a 20-listener study for comparison.
entries.condition: This is a count for prior work [10], not the target paper's MTurk study.

entries.text: The [10] comparison column reports 40.0% audio-only word intelligibility.
entries.condition: Published [10] comparator in Table 2; target text frames the comparison around S4, but does not restate [10]'s split, decoding, or listener-level protocol.

entries.text: The [10] comparison column reports 51.9% audio-visual word intelligibility.
entries.condition: Published [10] comparator in Table 2; target text frames the comparison around S4, but does not restate [10]'s split, decoding, or listener-level protocol.

entries.text: The target model reports 82.6% audio-only word intelligibility for S4, against 40.0% for [10].
entries.condition: Ours, S4 female; random 80/20 split; reconstructed audio only; GRID-vocabulary word choice by MTurk listeners; chance 19%
entries.quote: Audio-only 40.0% 82.6%

entries.text: The target model reports 79.9% audio-visual word intelligibility for S4.
entries.condition: Ours, S4 female; random 80/20 split of 1,000 S4 videos with all 51 GRID words in both sets; original video plus reconstructed audio; GRID-vocabulary forced choice; aggregate study used 23 workers and over 400 videos; chance is 19%; seed, repeated-run variance, and per-condition sample count are not reported.
entries.quote: Audio-visual 51.9% 79.9% 79%

entries.text: The target model reports 79% audio-visual word intelligibility after retraining/testing on S2.
entries.condition: Ours retrained on GRID speaker S2 (male); audio-visual only, using the same listening methodology; split size, random seed, repeated runs, and per-condition sample count are not stated; aggregate study used 23 workers; chance for GRID word choices is 19%.

entries.text: The authors claim their reconstructed speech is significantly more intelligible than the best [10] results on both listening configurations.
entries.condition: The stated claim is supported by the Table 2 comparison; no inferential test is described.
entries.quote:
Our recon-
structed audio is signiﬁcantly more intelligible than the best
results of [10], as shown by both audio-only and audio-visual
tests.

entries.text: The paper states that random guessing among GRID word categories yields 19% intelligibility.
entries.condition: Randomly choose a word from each GRID category; human evaluation uses the GRID vocabulary.
entries.quote: Randomly guessing a word from each GRID category would result in 19% “intelligibility”.

entries.text: The target paper does not provide the [10] comparator's exact train/test split, random seed, model-selection data, listener allocation, or decoding/LM conditions.
entries.condition: The text says its own experiments use S4 as in [10], but does not restate the comparator's full protocol.

entries.text: For OOV evaluation, the authors use five train/test splits, holding out two distinct digits from training in each split.
entries.unit: splits; digits held out per split
entries.condition: Digits held out of training are the test targets; one example trains on digits 1–8 and tests on 9 and 0.
entries.quote:
was trained and tested on ﬁve different train/test splits - each
with two distinct digits left out of the training set.

entries.text: Held-out digit audio-visual intelligibility is 51.6% averaged across the five OOV splits.
entries.condition: OOV audio-visual; two digits withheld per split; average across five train/test splits; listeners choose from the GRID vocabulary; chance is 10%; random seed and run variability are not reported.
entries.quote: Audio-visual 51.6% 93 .4% 10 .0%

entries.text: The Table 3 no-digits-held-out audio-visual condition reports 93.4% digit accuracy.
entries.condition: GRID digits are represented in training; audio-visual human word-choice evaluation. The paper does not specify a separate split or per-condition sample count for this row.
entries.quote: Audio-visual 51.6% 93 .4% 10 .0%

entries.text: The paper gives 10.0% as chance accuracy for digit guessing.
entries.condition: Random choice among the ten GRID digit options (0–9).
entries.quote: Audio-visual 51.6% 93 .4% 10 .0%

entries.text: The OOV score is obtained by averaging digit annotation accuracies across the five train/test splits.
entries.condition: The paper reports an average, not per-split scores or dispersion.

entries.text: The authors argue that listeners were over five times more likely than chance to choose the correct held-out digit, making regression promising for OOV reconstruction.
entries.condition: Based on 51.6% OOV accuracy versus the stated 10% digit chance level.

entries.text: The authors note OOV accuracy is only slightly more than half the all-digits-trained accuracy and suggest a larger, more diverse training vocabulary may improve it.
entries.condition: OOV audio-visual accuracy is compared with the Table 3 no-digits-held-out condition; the vocabulary-improvement statement is prospective.
entries.quote:
only slightly more than half as likely compared to having all
digits represented in the training set.

entries.text: The OOV protocol does not report random seeds, per-split results, repeated-run variability, validation/model-selection data, or per-condition annotation counts.
entries.condition: Five digit-leaveout splits are stated, but their generation and selection details are not.

entries.text: The model predicts continuous acoustic features and synthesizes audio; no text decoder or language model is described, although human listeners receive the GRID vocabulary.
entries.condition: Distinguish system-time processing from the closed-choice vocabulary supplied to MTurk listeners.

entries.text: The authors say spectrogram-magnitude output resynthesizes poorly because phase is absent, while raw-waveform output was rejected for lack of a suitable training loss.
entries.condition: Motivation for selecting an LPC/LSP acoustic target representation.

entries.text: The authors concede that 8th-order LPC is relatively low for high-fidelity speech-spectrum modeling; they retain it to isolate the visual-feature comparison with [10].
entries.condition: Audio targets use 8th-order LPC followed by LSP decomposition.

entries.text: Predicting excitation is out of scope; Gaussian white noise yields unvoiced, unnatural-sounding speech.
entries.condition: Waveform is synthesized from predicted LPC/LSP filter features plus Gaussian white-noise excitation.
entries.quote: This produces an unvoiced speech signal and results in unnatural sounding speech.

entries.text: The authors characterize their waveform-generation method as simplistic but say it works for their intelligibility-focused objective.
entries.condition: This does not establish naturalness or broader perceptual quality.

entries.text: The illustrated reconstructed audio lacks voiced-speech formants because the excitation is unvoiced.
entries.condition: Figure 3 shows LSP coefficients, waveform, and spectrogram examples.

entries.text: The authors suggest possible applications in noisy videoconferencing, conversation using wearable cameras/earpieces, and surveillance listening.
entries.condition: Motivating use cases only; no deployment or field evaluation is reported.

entries.text: The authors identify less-constrained video and speaker-independent/multiple-speaker reconstruction as future research needed to establish real-world viability and generalization.
entries.condition: Current experiments use constrained GRID data and train/test within individual speakers; S2 is separately retrained.

entries.text: No user confirmation step is described; the system's reported output is synthesized speech evaluated by a listening study.
entries.condition: No user acknowledgment or confirmation protocol is specified.

entries.text: Despite calling the [10] difference significant, the paper reports no statistical test, p-value, confidence interval, or uncertainty estimate for the comparison.
entries.condition: Table 2 provides point estimates only; no inferential method is described in the text.
entries.quote:
Our recon-
structed audio is signiﬁcantly more intelligible than the best
results of [10], as shown by both audio-only and audio-visual
tests.

entries.text: No user correction mechanism, correction data, or feedback-based model update is described.
entries.condition: The paper evaluates reconstruction with a listening study and reports no interactive correction phase.

entries.text: The paper does not report recording-session IDs or a session-wise/grouped split, so session overlap between train and test cannot be assessed.
entries.condition: The stated main split is random over videos from S4; only speaker identity, not session grouping, is described.

entries.text: The full-dataset train and test partitions each contain all 51 GRID words.

entries.condition: This is the vocabulary coverage condition for the random S4 80/20 split.

entries.text: GRID sentences follow a six-word grammar with command, color, preposition, letter, digit, and adverb positions.

entries.text: Two fully connected layers each have 512 neurons.
entries.condition: These follow the five convolutional blocks.

entries.text: The CNN output layer has 18 units, matching the acoustic feature vector.
entries.condition: The model predicts the 18-dimensional LSP-derived feature vector.

entries.text: The CNN is trained by backpropagation using mean squared error loss.
entries.condition: The target is the LSP-derived 18-dimensional vector.

entries.text: Weights are initialized with the procedure suggested by He et al.
entries.condition: The cited method is reference [18].

entries.text: Leaky ReLU is used in all but the last two layers; the last two layers use tanh.

questions.q: Which intelligibility figures belong to this paper, and what is the comparison baseline?
questions.answer: The paper's S4 model reports 82.6% audio-only and 79.9% audio-visual; S2 retrained audio-visual reports 79%. The [10] comparison column reports 40.0% and 51.9%, respectively. The paper claims superiority but gives no statistical test.

questions.q: How strong is the OOV-digit result, and what does it establish?
questions.answer: Across five splits with two digits held out per split, audio-visual digit accuracy is 51.6% versus 10.0% chance, while the no-digits-held-out condition is 93.4%. This is evidence of held-out-digit recognition under GRID's constrained vocabulary, not open-ended speech generalization.

questions.q: What does the face-versus-mouth result measure, and can it be reproduced from the reported protocol?
questions.answer: The best full-face test error is reported as 40% below the best mouth-region error at K=9. The figure's test split, error definition, selection procedure, and seed are not given.

questions.q: Which evaluation details remain unavailable for reproducing the headline results?
questions.answer: The main S4 split is random 80/20, but its seed and repeat count are absent; validation-set construction and session grouping are unspecified. Normalization formulas are stated, but the source partition for their statistics is not. The per-condition MTurk sample counts and statistical significance procedure are also missing.

questions.q: Does the system use a language model or interactive user correction?
questions.answer: The described system regresses continuous acoustic features and synthesizes a waveform; no text decoder, language model, confirmation step, or correction loop is described. MTurk listeners are given the GRID vocabulary for closed-choice evaluation.

questions.q: What limitations do the authors themselves identify?
questions.answer: They acknowledge unvoiced, unnatural-sounding synthesis and identify less-constrained video plus speaker-independent and multi-speaker reconstruction as future work.

questions.q: What is the audio-only S4 value in Table 2 (missing entry t35)?
questions.answer: 82.6% (Ours S4), against 40.0% for [10]; read by the writer from the Table 2 passage (grep), reader not run because the passage is two lines.

questions.q: Which Le Cornu and Milner (2015) configuration gives the 40.0% / 51.9% that Vid2speech compares against, and how did its listeners respond?
questions.answer: GMM UNV (GMM + AAM + 8th-order LPC, unvoiced excitation), Table 5; 20 listeners replayed clips and entered the words they heard (Sec. 5.2). Answered from the targeted passages of isca-cornu15-v2speech.

questions.q: How does Vid2speech score when re-run under one later protocol, and what is the best GRID value today?
questions.answer: Lip2Wav Table 2: Vid2Speech 44.92% WER against 14.08% for Lip2Wav (GRID, 4 speakers, Google ASR); Table 3 TCD-TIMIT 75.52% against 31.26%. Kefalas et al. 2023 Table IV: 4.07% (seen, 4 speakers); Table VII: 16.05% (unseen, 33 speakers).
